overview: This file documents the Freeport Sulphur Company’s July 1947 request to send technical representatives to occupied Japan to investigate sulphur deposits and potentially acquire operating rights. Company president Langbourne M. Williams, Jr. argued that Japanese production could alleviate a worldwide sulphur shortage, create employment, meet domestic requirements, and earn foreign exchange through exports. State Department correspondence and an internal memorandum show officials consulting the War Department, distinguishing the proposed mission from the newly authorized entry of ordinary traders, and considering a special permit from the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP). Although officials regarded expanded sulphur production favorably, they warned that economic instability had led the State Department to support a temporary moratorium on foreign investment in Japan.

subfiles.title: Freeport application to investigate Japanese sulphur deposits
subfiles.from: Langbourne M. Williams, Jr., President, Freeport Sulphur Company
subfiles.to: Robert A. Lovett, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Williams requests permission to send a small technical party to investigate Japanese sulphur deposits and assess the possibility of obtaining operating rights.
subfiles.summary: Freeport asks to send engineers to study Japan's sulphur deposits, arguing US-developed output could fill global demand and aid Japanese exports.

subfiles.title: Draft Lovett reply concerning the Freeport application
subfiles.about: Lovett advises Williams that the Department has prepared guidance and offers to arrange a Washington meeting if Freeport sends a representative.
subfiles.summary: Lovett tells Williams his sulphur inquiry was referred internally, offering to arrange a Washington meeting.

subfiles.title: Final Lovett reply inviting consultation in Washington
subfiles.from: Robert A. Lovett, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The final version of Lovett’s reply transmits departmental guidance and offers to arrange an official meeting in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Lovett repeats to Williams that his sulphur inquiry was referred, offering a Washington meeting if Freeport sends a representative.

subfiles.title: Martin memorandum on entry permits and foreign investment
subfiles.about: Martin assesses Freeport’s proposal, recommends interdepartmental discussions, and identifies restrictions on entry and foreign investment in occupied Japan.
subfiles.summary: Martin finds Freeport's sulphur mission doesn't fit standard entry rules, suggesting a meeting before seeking a special SCAP permit.

interest: Shows an American firm's bid to study Japanese sulphur deposits, caught between export-recovery goals and an investment moratorium.
